lead: This unit measures information and then spends it carefully. You will compute entropy and information rate, build Huffman codes, find the capacity of a channel, and design and decode the block and convolutional codes that push a real link towards that capacity.
about: The unit is about measuring information and then protecting it. Chapter 7.1 defines self-information, entropy and information rate. Chapter 7.2 uses entropy as the target that Shannon-Fano and Huffman codes try to reach, so the source is compressed. Chapter 7.3 moves from a source to a channel with mutual information, and 7.4 maximises it to get capacity and the Shannon-Hartley law. Chapter 7.5 states the channel coding theorem, which says capacity can be approached but not crossed. The rest of the unit is how engineers approach it: 7.6 linear block and Hamming codes with syndrome decoding, 7.7 cyclic codes and their polynomial encoders, 7.8 convolutional codes with Viterbi decoding, and 7.9 the modern BCH, turbo and LDPC codes.

chapters.idea: A symbol that is less likely carries more information, and the average information per symbol is the source entropy.
chapters.depth: Self-information I(xᵢ) = log₂(1/pᵢ) = −log₂ pᵢ bits, with pᵢ the probability of symbol i; show why the logarithm makes information from independent symbols add. Units: bit (base 2), nat (base e), hartley (base 10). Entropy H(X) = Σ pᵢ log₂(1/pᵢ) bits/symbol; maximum value log₂ M when all M symbols are equally likely; the binary entropy function H(p). Information rate R = r_s H bits/s, with r_s the symbol rate in symbols/s. Some syllabi call H the average information or the uncertainty of the source. Numerical drills on 4-level and 8-level sources only.

figure.aria: Plot of the binary entropy function H(p) against symbol probability p, rising from near zero at p = 0 to a peak of 1 bit at p = 0.5 and falling back to near zero at p = 1.

chapters.example: A source emits four symbols with probabilities 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and 1/8 at 2000 symbols per second. Find the information carried by each symbol, the source entropy and the information rate. Answers: 1 bit, 2 bits, 3 bits, 3 bits; H = 0.5(1) + 0.25(2) + 0.125(3) + 0.125(3) = 1.75 bits/symbol; R = 2000 × 1.75 = 3500 bit/s.
chapters.trap: Using log₁₀ or ln and still writing the answer in bits, and quoting a figure in bits per symbol when the question asks for bits per second.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: probability, random variables and the idea of a random source.
chapters.leave: Conditional and joint entropy to 7.3, code construction to 7.2, and noise models to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: Sort the symbol probabilities, build a binary tree that keeps the largest probabilities near the root, and the average codeword length comes close to the entropy.
chapters.depth: Prefix codes and instant decoding; the Kraft inequality stated without proof. Source coding theorem: H(X) ≤ L̄ < H(X) + 1 for a block code, with L̄ = Σ pᵢ lᵢ the average length in bits/symbol and lᵢ the length of codeword i. Shannon-Fano: sort probabilities in decreasing order, split into two groups of nearly equal total probability, give one group 0 and the other 1, repeat inside each group. Huffman: repeatedly merge the two smallest probabilities until one node is left, then read codes from the root. Efficiency η = H/L̄ and redundancy 1 − η. Run both methods on the same source and compare.

figure.aria: Huffman tree for the probabilities 0.4, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1 and 0.1, showing the merge steps and the codewords A = 0, B = 10, C = 110, D = 1110 and E = 1111.

chapters.example: A source has five symbols with probabilities 0.4, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1 and 0.1. Find the entropy, build a Huffman code, and find the average length and coding efficiency. Answers: H = 0.4 log₂2.5 + 2(0.2 log₂5) + 2(0.1 log₂10) = 2.12 bits/symbol. Merging 0.1+0.1 = 0.2, then 0.2+0.2 = 0.4, then 0.2+0.4 = 0.6, then 0.4+0.6 = 1.0 gives lengths 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, so L̄ = 0.4(1) + 0.2(2) + 0.2(3) + 0.1(4) + 0.1(4) = 2.2 bits/symbol and η = 2.12/2.2 = 96.5%. A Shannon-Fano split of the same probabilities gives the same code here.
chapters.trap: Splitting an unsorted probability list in Shannon-Fano, and reporting one symbol's codeword length as if it were the average length.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 7.1 for entropy and information rate.
chapters.leave: Channel coding and error correction to 7.5 onwards; the theorem itself to 7.5.

chapters.idea: Mutual information I(X;Y) is the part of the source uncertainty that the channel output removes.
chapters.depth: Joint entropy H(X,Y), conditional entropy H(X|Y) and H(Y|X), chain rule H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y|X). Mutual information I(X;Y) = H(X) − H(X|Y) = H(Y) − H(Y|X) = H(X) + H(Y) − H(X,Y); symmetry, I ≥ 0 and I ≤ min(H(X),H(Y)). Discrete memoryless channel: input alphabet, output alphabet, transition probabilities P(y|x) written as a channel matrix, memoryless meaning each output depends only on the input at that instant. Binary symmetric channel with crossover probability p: H(Y|X) = H(p), so I(X;Y) = H(Y) − H(p). One line on the binary erasure channel and its erasure probability. Some syllabi call I the average mutual information; the information rate through the channel is r_s I bits/s.

figure.aria: Venn diagram of the source entropy H(X) and output entropy H(Y) whose overlap is the mutual information I(X;Y), with H(X|Y) and H(Y|X) in the non-overlapping parts.

chapters.example: A binary symmetric channel has crossover probability p = 0.1 and the input symbols are equally likely. Find H(X), H(Y|X), H(Y), I(X;Y) and the information rate at 1000 symbols per second. Answers: H(X) = 1 bit; H(Y|X) = H(0.1) = 0.1 log₂10 + 0.9 log₂(1/0.9) = 0.469 bits; the output is also equally likely so H(Y) = 1 bit; I(X;Y) = 1 − 0.469 = 0.531 bits/symbol; rate = 531 bit/s.
chapters.trap: Swapping H(X|Y) with H(Y|X), and claiming I(X;Y) can be larger than H(X) or H(Y).
chapters.prereq: Chapter 7.1 for entropy; Unit 1 for conditional probability.
chapters.leave: Maximising I over the input distribution to 7.4; error correction to 7.5 onwards.

chapters.idea: Channel capacity is the largest mutual information any input distribution can produce, and for a band-limited AWGN channel it equals B log₂(1 + S/N).
chapters.depth: C = max over p(x) of I(X;Y) bits per channel use. BSC: C = 1 − H(p) bits/use, reached with equally likely inputs; C = 0 at p = 0.5, and C = 1 at p = 0 and also at p = 1 because a perfect inverter is usable. Erasure channel C = 1 − p_e in one line. Shannon-Hartley law: C = B log₂(1 + S/N) bits/s, B the channel bandwidth in Hz and S/N the signal-to-noise power ratio; convert from decibels with S/N = 10^(SNR(dB)/10). Capacity per hertz; what happens as B grows without limit, C → 1.44 S/N₀ with N₀ the noise power spectral density in W/Hz. The Shannon limit near −1.6 dB in Eb/N₀ quoted in one line with no derivation. Some syllabi call this Shannon's channel capacity theorem or the Shannon-Hartley law.

figure.aria: Plot of capacity per hertz C/B against signal-to-noise ratio in decibels, rising as log₂(1 + S/N) from about 0.14 bit/s/Hz at −10 dB to nearly 10 bit/s/Hz at 30 dB.

chapters.example: A telephone channel has bandwidth B = 3.1 kHz and SNR = 30 dB. Find the capacity, and repeat for SNR = 20 dB. Answers: 30 dB gives S/N = 1000, so C = 3100 × log₂(1001) = 3100 × 9.97 = 30.9 kbit/s. At 20 dB, S/N = 100, log₂(101) = 6.66, so C = 3100 × 6.66 = 20.6 kbit/s. A BSC with p = 0.01 has C = 1 − H(0.01) = 1 − 0.081 = 0.919 bit per channel use.
chapters.trap: Putting the decibel value straight into log₂(1 + S/N), and mixing bits per second with bits per channel use.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 7.3 for mutual information; Unit 1 for AWGN and noise power spectral density.
chapters.leave: How to build codes that reach C to 7.5 to 7.9; modulation bandwidth efficiency to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: For any rate below capacity a code exists that makes the error probability as small as we like, and above capacity no code can.
chapters.depth: Statement of the channel coding theorem for a discrete memoryless channel: for rate R = k/n below C there are codes of length n with error probability tending to zero as n grows; the converse for R > C. What it promises (existence, long blocks) and what it does not (no construction, no bound on delay or decoder complexity). Random-coding and typical-sequence reasoning in one short paragraph, no heavy counting. Code rate, redundancy 1 − R, and coding gain in dB at a fixed error rate. The elementary coding techniques some syllabi ask for: repetition code, single parity check, and why they help. Tie back to the BSC capacity of 7.4.

figure.aria: Block diagram of a coded link: k message bits enter an (n,k) encoder, the n coded bits pass through a noisy channel, and the decoder outputs an estimate of the k message bits.

chapters.example: A binary symmetric channel has p = 0.01. Each bit is sent three times and the receiver takes a majority vote. Find the code rate, the decoded bit error probability, and check the rate against capacity. Answers: R = 1/3. A bit is wrong after decoding when two or three of the three copies are wrong: P = 3p²(1 − p) + p³ = 3(0.0001)(0.99) + 0.000001 = 2.98 × 10⁻⁴, against 10⁻² uncoded. Capacity is 1 − H(0.01) = 0.919, and 1/3 < 0.919, so the theorem allows this gain.
chapters.trap: Expecting the theorem to hand over a specific code, and believing a clever enough decoder can push the error to zero above capacity.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 7.4 for capacity; Unit 1 for probability of independent bit errors.
chapters.leave: The actual code families to 7.6 to 7.9.

chapters.idea: A linear block code is a subspace: encoding is multiplication by G, and the syndrome rHᵀ names the error pattern rather than the received word.
chapters.depth: (n,k) code, code rate k/n, Hamming weight and distance, minimum distance d_min. Detection of up to d_min − 1 errors and correction of t = ⌊(d_min − 1)/2⌋ errors. Generator matrix G in systematic form [Iₖ | P] with P a k × (n−k) block; parity check matrix H = [Pᵀ | Iₙ₋ₖ]; GHᵀ = 0 and c = mG. Syndrome s = rHᵀ = eHᵀ, the syndrome table and single-error correction; the standard array in one line. Hamming code (7,4): d_min = 3, t = 1, the columns of H are the seven non-zero 3-bit words, Hamming bound 2^(n−k) ≥ 1 + n, perfect code. Say in words how the encoder and syndrome calculator are wired.

figure.aria: Flow of the Hamming (7,4) example: message 1011 becomes codeword 1011010, one bit flips to give 1010010, the syndrome 111 points to error pattern 0001000, and correction gives back 1011010.

chapters.example: For the (7,4) Hamming code take G = [I₄ | P] with rows of P equal to 110, 101, 011 and 111. (a) Encode m = 1011. (b) Flip the fourth bit of the codeword and decode it. Answers: (a) adding rows 1, 3 and 4 of G gives c = 1011010. (b) r = 1010010; s₁ = 1, s₂ = 1, s₃ = 1 so s = 111, which is column 4 of H, so e = 0001000 and the corrected word is 1011010.
chapters.trap: Reading the syndrome as the decimal error position, and forgetting that d_min = 3 means two errors are detected but only one is corrected.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 7.5 for why codes are used; Unit 1 for modulo-2 arithmetic basics.
chapters.leave: Cyclic structure to 7.7, multiple-error codes to 7.9, and soft-decision detection to 7.8.

chapters.idea: A cyclic code is a linear block code closed under cyclic shifts, so every codeword is a multiple of a generator polynomial and encoding is polynomial division.
chapters.depth: Cyclic shift property, codewords as polynomials c(x) = c₀ + c₁x + … + c_{n−1}x^(n−1) over GF(2), addition is XOR. Generator polynomial g(x) of degree n − k that divides xⁿ + 1, so k = n − deg g; non-systematic c(x) = m(x)g(x). Systematic encoding: divide x^(n−k)m(x) by g(x), the remainder is the parity block, c(x) = x^(n−k)m(x) + remainder. Parity check polynomial h(x) = (xⁿ + 1)/g(x). Syndrome is the remainder of r(x) ÷ g(x); it is zero for a valid codeword and depends only on e(x). Describe the shift-register encoder and the syndrome calculator stage by stage; some syllabi ask only these two. Run (7,4) with g(x) = x³ + x + 1 throughout.

figure.aria: Systematic encoder flow: message 1101 is shifted by x³, divided by g(x) = x³ + x + 1, leaves remainder 001, and the codeword is 1101001.

chapters.example: A (7,4) cyclic code uses g(x) = x³ + x + 1. (a) Encode the message 1101 systematically. (b) Find the syndrome when the received word has a single error in the x⁴ position. Answers: (a) m(x) = x³ + x² + 1, x³m(x) = x⁶ + x⁵ + x³; dividing by g(x) leaves remainder 1, so the parity bits are 001 and c = 1101001. (b) error e(x) = x⁴, and x³ ≡ x + 1, so x⁴ ≡ x² + x and the syndrome is 110, a non-zero remainder that flags an error.
chapters.trap: Using a g(x) that does not divide xⁿ + 1, and attaching the remainder bits on the left of the message instead of the right.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 7.6 for linear block codes and syndromes; polynomial long division over GF(2).
chapters.leave: BCH codes, which are cyclic codes with several roots, to 7.9.

chapters.idea: A convolutional code spreads each input bit over several output bits through a shift register, and Viterbi decoding picks the trellis path closest to the received sequence.
chapters.depth: (n,k,K) notation with constraint length K = memory + 1; rate R = k/n. Rate 1/2, K = 3 encoder with generator sequences g₁ = 111 and g₂ = 101, drawn as a two-stage shift register with two modulo-2 adders. State diagram, code tree and trellis; free distance. Viterbi algorithm: branch metric as Hamming distance for hard decisions, add-compare-select at each state, survivor paths, traceback, complexity growing as 2^(K−1) states. Terminating the trellis with K − 1 zero bits. One line that soft-decision decoding adds about 2 dB. No Viterbi proof.

figure.aria: State diagram of the rate 1/2, K = 3 convolutional encoder with four states 00, 10, 01 and 11, each edge labelled with the input bit followed by the two output bits.

chapters.example: A rate 1/2, K = 3 convolutional encoder uses g₁ = 111 and g₂ = 101. (a) Encode the message 1011 followed by two zero flush bits. (b) The received word has bit 7 flipped; decode and give the surviving path metric. Answers: (a) the outputs are 11 10 00 01 01 11, so the transmitted word is 111000010111. (b) the received word is 111000110111, which differs from the transmitted word in one bit; Viterbi keeps the path 00 → 10 → 01 → 10 → 11 → 01 → 00 with metric 1, so the decoded message is 1011.
chapters.trap: Treating the constraint length as the memory, and forgetting the K − 1 flush bits so the trellis never returns to the zero state.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 7.6 for parity and distance ideas; Unit 5 for maximum-likelihood detection.
chapters.leave: Iterative and sparse-graph decoding to 7.9; passband modulation of coded bits to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: BCH, turbo and LDPC codes are the practical codes that come within a fraction of a decibel of the Shannon limit by using long blocks and soft iterative decoding.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this, so keep it short and descriptive. BCH: a t-error-correcting cyclic code over GF(2^m) with n = 2^m − 1 and d_min ≥ 2t + 1, examples (15,7) with t = 2 and (15,5) with t = 3; Reed-Solomon as the non-binary relative used on discs and QR codes in one line. Turbo: two recursive systematic convolutional encoders in parallel with an interleaver, natural rate 1/3 punctured to 1/2, iterative MAP or SOVA decoding. LDPC: sparse parity check matrix, Tanner graph, belief propagation, very large n, used in Wi-Fi and 5G data channels. One comparison line on latency, complexity and how close each sits to capacity. No bit-level decoding algorithms.

figure.aria: Turbo encoder: the input block feeds one RSC encoder directly and a second one through an interleaver, and the multiplexer sends out the systematic bit with both parity streams.

chapters.example: A link is offered a BCH (15,7) code and a turbo code. (a) For the BCH code find n, k, the number of correctable errors, the minimum distance, the code rate, and check the Hamming bound. (b) The turbo encoder uses two rate-1/2 RSC encoders and sends the systematic bit with both parity bits; find the rate, then the rate after puncturing every second parity bit. Answers: (a) n = 15, k = 7, t = 2, d_min ≥ 5, R = 7/15 = 0.467; correctable patterns 1 + 15 + 105 = 121 ≤ 2⁸ = 256, so the bound holds. (b) 3 output bits per input bit give rate 1/3; puncturing halves the parity bits to 1 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 2 bits per input bit, so the rate becomes 1/2.
chapters.trap: Thinking a strong code can beat capacity, and confusing code rate with redundancy when the puncturing pattern is given.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 7.4 to 7.8 for capacity, Hamming distance and convolutional encoders.
chapters.leave: Detailed iterative decoding mathematics to a later course; modulation and channel models to Units 5 and 6.
